docs.title: Theatre Notes
docs.text: Professional theatre practice and the venue records that go with it.

docs.title: What is here
docs.text:
Venues are records of one building: its circuits, its rooms, its numbers. Practice is the craft, the part that is true regardless of which building you are standing in.

Both live here, and the boundary runs between pages rather than between repos. That is deliberate: a venue page should be able to link to the general practice instead of restating it and then slowly disagreeing with the last place that restated it.

  • Ogunquit Playhouse — venue records, electrics
  • Paper tech — general practice

docs.title: Paper tech
docs.text:
Walking every cue in the prompt book with the design team before anybody is standing on stage waiting.

This page exists as the first real content on this site and as a demonstration: it is a procedure, it names an owner, and the table above is drawn from its frontmatter by the type rather than typed by hand.

The cost of skipping it

Every cue not agreed on paper gets agreed in the room instead, with the full company on the clock. It is the cheapest hour in the process and the easiest one to cut.

docs.title: Why it is general and not venue-specific
docs.text:
Nothing above names a building. That is the test for whether a page belongs on this site: a venue's page can link here for the practice and add only what is true of its own room.

docs.title: Ogunquit Playhouse
docs.text:
Venue records. Currently electrics only; other departments arrive as their paperwork gets written up.

Why a venue lives on a general-practice site

This site holds both, and the boundary runs between PAGES rather than between repos: a practice page describes how a thing is generally done, a venue page records what is true of one building. Sitting them side by side is the point, because a venue page should be able to link to the practice instead of restating it.

docs.title: Circuits and dimmers
docs.text:
The rack schedule: every soca run out of the three dimmer racks and the two ML panels, what it is called, and where it lands.

This is the reference you trace backwards from a dead fixture. Find the circuit number, read the rack letter, and the colour column tells you which loom to follow in the rack itself.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
The rack rows are section breaks, not records. RACK 1, ML PANEL 2 and so on divide the sheet; everything under one belongs to it until the next.

The first column stays put when you scroll sideways, and so does the header, so a value eight columns to the right still tells you what it is and which circuit it belongs to. On a phone, swipe the table rather than turning it.

Blanks mean unknown, not empty

A blank destination is a run nobody has traced, not a run that goes nowhere. No Soca in the notes column is different and does mean what it says: the dimmer exists in the rack with no soca run out of it.

docs.title: Where the dimmers run
docs.text:
The field survey: what each circuit is currently on, walked and recorded in July 2024, as against what the rack schedule says it should be.

Two documents rather than one, on purpose. The rack schedule is the design; this is the observation. Merging them would quietly overwrite one with the other and destroy the only thing that makes either useful, which is being able to see where they disagree.

This is a dated snapshot

Every row is true as of the walk. A house this size re-patches constantly, so treat anything here as a strong lead rather than a fact, and verify before you cut power to something.

docs.title: The asterisks and question marks are deliberate
docs.text:
R27?? and R3zAA * (unlisted on label) are the surveyor's own uncertainty, preserved exactly as written. Do not clean them up. A marked doubt is information; the same cell tidied into a confident value is a trap for whoever reads it next.
